section_title: Why does Jesus face arrest while everyone else flees?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 43 While Jesus was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived, accompanied by a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. 44 Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him and lead Him away securely.” 45 Going directly to Jesus, he said, “Rabbi!” and kissed Him. 46 Then the men seized Jesus and arrested Him. 47 And one of the bystanders drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.

48 Jesus asked the crowd, “Have you come out with swords and clubs to arrest Me as you would an outlaw? 49 Every day I was with you, teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me. But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.” 50 Then everyone deserted Him and fled. 51 One young man who had been following Jesus was wearing a linen cloth around his body. They caught hold of him, 52 but he pulled free of the linen cloth and ran away naked.

context_lines: While Jesus is still speaking about the approaching betrayal, Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the religious authorities. He has arranged a kiss as the signal identifying Jesus. A greeting that would ordinarily express closeness becomes the means of handing Him over.

The Greek verb for the kiss is καταφιλέω (kataphileō, kah-tah-fee-LEH-oh), which can mean to kiss warmly or repeatedly. The word makes the use of affection as a sign of betrayal especially painful, but it does not tell us how long the kiss lasted. ([Thayer, καταφιλέω](https://biblehub.com/greek/2705.htm))

Someone nearby draws a sword and cuts off the high priest’s servant’s ear. John identifies the attacker as Peter and the servant as Malchus, while Luke records Jesus healing the injury. Mark emphasizes Jesus’ question: why arrest Him like an outlaw when He has taught openly in the temple? He then places what is happening within the fulfillment of Scripture. ([John 18:1–11](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/18.htm); [Luke 22:47–53](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/22.htm))

Everyone deserts Him. Even a young man who has been following escapes only by leaving his linen covering behind. Mark does not name him. The scene leaves Jesus in custody as the others flee, bringing the earlier warning about their failure into view.
common_interpretation_lines: Christian readers commonly see Jesus willingly facing the suffering ahead while His followers fail to remain with Him. The young man’s identity remains uncertain; Calvin rejects confident identification and takes his seizure as further evidence of the crowd’s violence. ([Calvin, Mark 14:51](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/14.htm))
god_plan_lines: Isaiah’s suffering servant is rejected and led like a lamb to slaughter, yet bears the sins of others. Peter explicitly applies that servant language to Christ: He does not retaliate under abuse and carries sins in His body so that His people may live rightly. Jesus’ submission here belongs to that saving path, not to a lack of authority to resist. ([Isaiah 53:4–12](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/53.htm); [1 Peter 2:21–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/2.htm))

Peter also describes Jesus as the Shepherd to whom wandering people return. That supplies the wider hope behind this scene of abandonment: the One left alone goes on to give His life for people who need to be brought back to God. ([1 Peter 2:24–25](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/2.htm))
